title: Bates v. C & S Adjusters, Inc. (1992)
summary: Venue was proper where the allegedly unlawful collection letter was received, even though the collector originally mailed it to another state.
notes:
This is not a rule that a plaintiff may always sue at home. The source identifies a concrete claim-generating event in the district. The case illustrates why venue and personal jurisdiction must be analyzed separately.

Bates incurred the debt while living in the Western District of Pennsylvania and C & S was a local Pennsylvania collection agency doing no regular business in New York; the Postal Service forwarded the unmarked notice to Bates's new Western District of New York address, and the Second Circuit reversed and remanded under the 1990 amendment to 28 U.S.C. section 1391 (a district where a substantial part of the events giving rise to the claim occurred), reasoning that the harm from an abusive collection notice occurs on receipt.

sections.Parties: Bates sued C & S Adjusters under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.
sections.Material Facts: The collector sent a collection letter to an address in Pennsylvania. The letter was forwarded to Bates in New York, where he received it. The collector had not necessarily intended that forwarding. Bates alleged that the communication violated federal debt-collection law, making the location where it reached him relevant to the claim.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed for improper venue. The Second Circuit reversed, construing the statute’s substantial-events provision.
sections.Issue: Could the district where the forwarded collection notice arrived qualify as a district in which a substantial part of the events giving rise to the claim occurred?
sections.Holding: Yes. Receipt of the letter was a substantial event in the alleged statutory violation.
sections.Reasoning: The venue statute did not require identifying a single district with the most significant contacts or proving that every relevant act occurred in the chosen district. The alleged harm associated with an improper debt-collection communication could occur where it was received. That event mattered to the cause of action even though the collector had mailed the letter elsewhere. A jurisdictional inquiry into purposeful forum conduct would ask a different question. The Court did not resolve a contested personal-jurisdiction issue by holding venue proper.

learning.why: Venue was proper where the allegedly unlawful collection letter was received, even though the collector originally mailed it to another state.

topics.cp-venue: Receipt of a collection letter could be a substantial event giving rise to the statutory claim. The court’s venue inquiry was separate from personal jurisdiction.
topics.cp-personal-jurisdiction: Venue did not depend on showing that the collector deliberately arranged the letter’s forwarding.
topics.cp-usc-1391: The case construes the 'substantial part of the events' language added to section 1391(b)(2) in 1990.
topics.cp-statute-interpretation: The Second Circuit read the amended venue statute to focus on where the harm occurred rather than the defendant's intent.

mnemonic.rationale: A collection letter forwarded to New York
